newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire slides into new war, U.S. worried.
newsitem.headline: Zaire slides into new war, U.S. worried.

text.p: Inhabitants of outlying areas of Kisangani on Friday reported fighting northeast of the Zairean city where the army, backed by mercenaries, has based its operation to retake territory from rebels.
Renewed fighting in eastern Zaire which has been wracked by violence since Tutsi-led rebels took up arms against the army last October has sent alarm bells ringing in world capitals.
The United States said it was profoundly worried by signs of a new explosion of violence in Zaire, a development it said could lead to clashes between national armies in the region.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR sounded a warning on Friday of a possible humanitarian catastrophe, while France denied any link with French mercenaries reported backing the Zaire army.
Residents around Kisangani, a jungle city now bustling with military activity, said there was fighting on Thursday in Wamba about 300 km (180 miles) to the northeast.
There was no official confirmation from the military high command, which retains almost total silence on operational details of the government's drive against rebels.
"We are hearing reports of heavy shooting at Wamba. We don't know who the fighting is between," said one Kisangani resident who was in radio contact with the town.

Other well-informed sources in Kisangani who asked not to be named, said Zaire this week used recently acquired Russian combat helicopters flown by foreign pilots to bombard rebels near a bridge around 250 km (155 miles) southeast of Kisangani.
The bridge is on one of the few passable roads leading to the rebel-occupied eastern towns of Goma and Bukavu.

They said dozens of wounded soldiers had been brought into Kisangani in recent weeks. The casualties were either from attacks on Zairean positions or from attempts by government forces to infiltrate rebel held areas.
Prime Minister Kengo Wa Dondo gave the green light on Monday for the start of a much-touted counter-offensive.
But there have been no confirmed reports of a mass movement of troops for the "total and devastating" counter-attack the government says it intends to carry out.

However, in Kisangani the military has visibly built up its arsenal ahead of the intended campaign. Mortars, crates of ammunition, as well as six combat helicopters and two small fighter jets are all visible on the tarmac at the airport.
The army will also be backed by up to 300 foreign mercenaries, according to people following the buildup.
White mercenaries, armed and in combat uniforms, can be seen in Kisangani driving around in jeeps alongside Zairean soldiers.
Western sources say that the ercenaries are a motley crew, originating, from numerous European countries including France and Belgium but mainly from the former Yugoslavia.
French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said on Friday there were only five French military staff in Zaire -- the embassy's defence attache and four security guards.

"If it were verified that French nationals were working as mercenaries in Zaire in a private capacity, such activities could only be condemned in the clearest way as they do not correspond in any way to French policy," he told reporters.
The left-wing French daily Liberation said on Friday some 280 European soldiers of fortune, including several Frenchmen, were in east Zaire under the command of a Belgian mercenary.
Zaire denies hiring mercenaries to fight, saying there are only a handful of military instructors sent by foreign allies.

But Zairean intelligence sources in Kinshasa, contradicting the official line, said the bulk of the mercenaries had already been sent to areas near rebel-held territory. They named the town of Watsa in the north, and Kalemie and Kindu in the south.
Mercenaries first started arriving in late December, according to Kisangani residents.
The Zaire army's ragged uniforms have now been replaced with brand new combat fatigues and discipline has improved.
Deserting soldiers looted the town and terrorised residents in November and December.

But most Zaireans agree the army's ability to push back rebels may depend in large on whether neighbouring Uganda and Rwanda intervene. Both states and army-ruled Burundi are accused by Zaire of backing ethnic Tutsis who originally launched the rebellion after local authoririties threatened to expel them.
